docs.title: From bland to bold: turning any image into a vector with Vexy Lines
docs.text:
A photograph is not a vector. A sketch is not a vector. A scanned logo is definitely not a vector. Vexy Lines exists to fix that, one image at a time.

The promise is simple: hand Vexy Lines a sketched drawing, a photograph, a scan, or anything you generated with an AI tool, and it returns a scalable vector you can actually use. SVG, EPS, PDF, PNG, JPG — take your pick. The less simple part is everything that happens in between.

Vexy Lines does not just trace edges. It applies halftone patterns, dithering effects, stipple designs and linear engraving styles. The output looks deliberate, not mechanical.

That matters in practice. Screen printers need artwork that separates cleanly. Muralists need files that scale to a wall without going soft. Tattoo artists need line work that holds at small sizes and prints well on skin. None of these people want an auto-traced blob. They want something that looks like it was drawn by someone who knew what they were doing.

Vexy Lines also supports variable fonts for line-based fills. Multicolor halftone and flowlines/trace fill round out the effect options. If you have spent time in Illustrator trying to fake these looks manually, the appeal is immediate.

The retrofuturistic use case is a good example of what the tool does well: take a photograph and turn it into something that looks like a Wall Street Journal hedcut portrait, or a 1970s technical illustration, or a letterpress-ready design. The kind of aesthetic that takes hours to approximate by hand and seconds to miss.

Vexy Lines runs on Mac and Windows. The price is US$99 — one payment, lifetime license, two devices. There is a free trial if you want to see what it does to your own images before committing.

The software is available now at vexy.art/lines. You can try it in the browser without installing anything via the online playground.

A bland image is, in the end, just a vector waiting for the right filter.

docs.title: Vexy Lines 2 is here!
docs.text:
Say hello to Vexy Lines 2, with all-new image filters, a stroke-cutting sharp mask, cross-hatching diamond dots, organic wobble & rough strokes, much faster parameter tweaking, and hundreds of other improvements. If you have Vexy Lines 1, it’s free!

In this article, we’re covering the new features in Vexy Lines 2.0, and also those that we added Vexy Lines 1.1. If you already have Vexy Lines, use Check for Updates to get the latest version. If you don’t, now is a good time!

docs.title: What’s Vexy Lines?
docs.text:
With Vexy Lines, you can transform your photos and bitmap images into infinitely scalable vector artwork.

From traditional autotrace, to engraving-style line art, retro halftone dot patterns, impactful spirals, wave textures, scribbles, wireframes, fractal curves—and even variable text, where typesetting dynamically picks variable font instances depending on the region of the underlying source image.

Start by applying a single fill for immediate results. Use masks to apply different fills on parts of the image. Add an extra dimension with a mesh. Then export or copy the result as a scalable SVG or PDF graphic, or as a PNG or JPEG.

Every fill transforms the source image into signal with filters, and from it generates pattern paths: lines or dots that form the skeleton of the fill. Then stroke parameters render the paths into strokes. Keep that chain in mind—signal, paths, strokes—because most of what’s new sharpens one link in it.

docs.title: New in 2.0: Image filters
docs.text:
Optimal stroke parameters are only half of impactful vector artwork—the signal itself matters just as much. The source image is the control surface for the finished artwork. When a fill turns your image into engraving lines, halftone dots, or hatching, the pixels decide how dense the pattern gets, where strokes thicken and thin, how the lines break and gather.

But you don’t easily see it upfront: a photo can look perfectly good on screen and still produce a muddy, clogged halftone or a thin, lifeless engraving.

Where 1.1 gave you brightness and contrast, 2.0 turns that into a full filter stack. New image postprocessing filters added on any fill change how that fill interprets the source image. Use the Filters section of the Properties panel to add, remove, or reorder filters on the current fill.

Nudge the contrast and watch the lines respond. Sharpen the source and watch the halftone tighten. Lift the shadows and watch detail appear in the dark areas of the pattern. You’re adjusting the signal and shaping the vectors. Finally, you can experiment until it’s right instead of exporting, re-importing, and hoping.

Adjust Brightness, Contrast, Levels, Shadows / Highlights. Sharpen or Blur. Invert the image or restrict its Color range.

Add a Gradient to a path-producing fill, base a Text fill on it, use a variable font, and watch weight or width change smoothly along the gradient. Or emphasize the foreground and fade the rest with Remove background—it uses an algorithm tuned to your platform and is never fast, so use it sparingly.

In the Image & Signal section, click the new Show source image to preview the postprocessed result, or use the Histogram to limit the final signal threshold.

docs.title: New in 2.0: Sharp masks
docs.text:
Each layer’s mask defines its active regions. The Normal mask cuts the pattern paths, which are then expanded into strokes—so those strokes can spill past the mask boundary. Smooth mask softens the signal gradually with a tolerance you set.

The new Sharp mask cuts the rendered strokes precisely at the mask boundaries. No spill.

And when Mask Overlay makes the current layer’s active regions inactive in the group’s layers below, those excluded regions now render correctly in red if Highlight Masks is on.

  • Updated in 1.1: With the Brush tool active, tap [ and ] to decrease or increase the mask brush size

docs.title: New in 2.0: Diamond dots
docs.text:
Say you have fills that together form a grid of small cells enclosed by crossing paths—for example, two Linear fills at different angles that intersect into diamond-shaped cells.

Select two or more such fills, choose Create Diamond Dots from the Fill menu, and Vexy Lines builds a new “Diamond Dots” fill. This new Handmade fill consists of short lines that run diagonally through each cell, with a short stroke—the “diamond dot” growing from the middle of each cell. Drag the end nodes of each line to adjust the line lengths, and in the Handmade Fill section decide how much of that length renders as the dot.

docs.title: New in 2.0: More organic strokes
docs.text:
The Stroke Thickness section gains two parameters you can combine:

Wobble adds hand-drawn pen jitter to the stroke. Rough adds high-frequency paper roughness. Together they take the mechanical edge off a vectorized line.

docs.title: New in 2.0: Drag parameter icons
docs.text: Whenever a numeric field in the Properties panel has an icon to the left of the number, you can press-and-hold the icon—a small captioned slider appears underneath. Drag the icon to change the value: a short drag tunes precisely, a longer drag moves faster. It works for fill parameters like interval and rotation, and stroke parameters like smoothing and thinning. (Real sliders, like opacity, stroke thickness, and the dashes line threshold, still work the way they always did.)

docs.title: New in 1.1: Flowlines fill
docs.text:
Flowlines is a Handmade Fill subtype where strokes follow a direction field generated from the image. They wrap around shapes and follow edges instead of cutting across them.

Imagine your source image is a terrain immersed in water. Auto Flowlines generates currents that cross and combine depending on the shape of the underwater terrain. Each stroke is a little paper ship that sails across the image, guided by those currents—following edges, wrapping around forms, changing direction where the image does.

Flowlines also works in manual mode: draw a few base lines with the Pencil tool and the currents reshape themselves to follow them, as if you dipped a stick into the water and traced a path. A Push Strength setting controls how strongly strokes continue through dense areas—higher values push deeper between neighbors, lower values stop earlier for a tighter result.

  • New in 2.0: Flowlines now finds edges more reliably.

docs.title: Updated in 1.1: Handmade fills
docs.text: Three similar Handmade fill kinds are now unified into one Extended subtype, with the joining method (miter, bevel, rounded) moved to a selector near the Stroke shift.

docs.title: New in 1.1: Stochastic Stippling fill
docs.text: Stochastic Stippling is a Halftone Fill subtype. It places dots so darker areas are denser and lighter areas are sparser, emulating the classic pen-and-ink stippling technique used in illustration, scientific diagrams, and editorial art. Because the placement is randomized rather than gridded—the same principle behind modern inkjet and fine-art printing—the result is softer and less mechanical than a regular dot grid.

docs.title: Updated in 1.1: Spiral fill
docs.text: Spiral Fill now lets you choose the direction of rotation: clockwise or counter-clockwise.

docs.title: Updated in 1.1: Fractal fill
docs.text: Fractal Fill got a real overhaul. You can now choose between two space-filling curve types: Huber (square-based) and Gosper (triangle-based). Pattern density moved to the familiar Interval selector instead of the old Depth parameter, and a new Sharp / Round corner selector controls how the curve bends at each turn.

docs.title: Updated: Fills and strokes
docs.text:
• Auto Thinning makes strokes thinner in crowded areas where many lines meet, reducing buildup in dense regions.
  • Fill rotation now allows fractional angles.
  • The ends of round-capped strokes draw more correctly on short or tightly-curved segments.
  • Dash by Thickness switches between continuous and dashed lines based on stroke thickness rather than image brightness—which pairs nicely with Auto Thinning, since thinned strokes can become dashed too.
  • Round dots and dashed caps render correctly where cutting lines cross dashed lines.
  • In multi-line Text fill, the first glyph of a line no longer disappears.
  • Type in the font picker and matching fonts list at the top, with the rest dimmed rather than hidden.

docs.title: New in 1.1: Export and file handling
docs.text:
In File > Export As, you choose the format (PDF, SVG, EPS, PNG, JPG), and the destination: clipboard, next to the document with the same base name, or a Save dialog.

After that, File > Export (Cmd+E / Ctrl+E) repeats the last export instantly. Handy for linked workflows and for quickly dropping an SVG or PNG into another app!

docs.title: Updated in 1.1 and 2.0: Interface and workflow
docs.text:
• In Preferences, you can choose light or dark UI mode.
  • Layers panel is faster, with easier drag-and-drop reordering and double-click renaming.
  • The canvas refreshes faster after you change fill parameters.
  • Handling of layers and groups in the Layers panel is greatly improved
  • Alt+drag of nodes is better
  • Dragging a selection snaps at the document edge
  • Properties panel has had numerous detailed touch-ups.
  • You can set a document background color in the Properties panel, included in PDF, SVG, and PNG exports.
  • On Windows, File Explorer now shows richer thumbnails and previews for .lines documents.

Plus hundreds of other improvements and fixes throughout the app.

Vexy Lines 2 is a free upgrade for everyone on version 1. Grab it with Check for Updates, and as always, tell us what you make with it—and what you’d like to see next.

docs.title: A new home for Vexy Lines where pixels become lines
docs.text:
In October 2025, we launched Vexy Lines, a Mac & Windows app that redraws any photo as editable vector line art: engraving, halftone, stipple, wireframe, even live variable type that reads the image beneath it. We just revamped the vexy.art/lines website, which now includes real-life case studies.

A dozen vector fills helps in your creation: Linear engraving, Wave, Halftone, Scribble, Wireframe, Fractal, the image-reading Text fill. Add layers, masks, filters, mesh warps, and you get machinery that turns a one-click result into a considered piece.

On the page, you’ll find case studies that showcase Vexy Lines in real-life (or at least plausible!) scenarios: team portraits with a sci-fi twist, pixel-driven variable typography, vector lettering that survives vinyl cutting, and a faithful, ultrasharp digital revival of a retro poster.

Say hello to Vexy Lines! →

docs.title: Type that reads the picture underneath it
docs.text:
With Vexy Lines, you can make the most of your variable fonts. Create expressive typographic arrangements, impactful headlines and font specimens. Check out the Vexy Lines Text fill! It typesets your text along the baselines created by the app’s procedural patterns. Each text glyph picks its font size or variable font instance from the brightness of the image beneath it. Sampled per glyph. Mapped to Weight, Width, Optical Size, or any other axis. Exported to SVG & PDF. For foundries who want to show their design spaces flow along pixels.

What do Vexy Lines and FontLab have in common? Same developers, and same passion for high-quality typography. Of course we added a unique typographic gem into our new parametric vector graphics creation app: Text fill!

Drop in a source image, Put a base fill over it, and hide it — Linear, Wave, Circular, Spiral, Handmade, or even Halftone!

Apply Filters like Contrast or Blur to the base fill to tweak the impact of the source image.

Add a Text fill based on the first fill. The pattern paths of the base fill decide where and how the baselines in the Text fill will flow. Enter your text, pick a variable font, nominate a variation axis.

As the text flows along the pattern paths, Vexy Lines samples the image brightness under each glyph, and makes two-fold use of it.

The image brightness modulates the stroke thickness within the thickness range in the hidden base fill. This, in turn, modulates the font size in the Text fill. Lighter pixels — thinner stroke — smaller glyphs. Make the min and max thickness the same for a constant font size.

Additionally, the image brightness directly drives the variable instance selection along the nominated axis, one interpolated instance per glyph. This works even if the min and max stroke thickness are the same. If you choose Weight, light pixels will give you light letters, dark pixels give you bold glyphs.

That makes it a specimen tool, not a gimmick. Instead of nine static cuts you get the full axis rendered continuously across a single word, and the axis can be anything your designspace defines — Weight, Width, Optical Size, a custom grade; the flame poem drives Weight, Width, Italic and Optical Size at once. It works with the real families you already license — Playfair by Claus Eggers Sørensen, Futura, whatever variable font you feed it — and it exports to SVG and PDF, so the finished piece drops straight into the specimen sheet or the deck you were already building.

Discover variable typography in Vexy Lines →

docs.title: Your face on your next crypto banknotes
docs.text:
Many headshots, many cameras, one team photoshoot: with Vexy Lines, you can turn low-quality photos into visually harmonized, crisp SVGs & PDFs. Turn your starship crew into WSJ-style hedcuts or brutalist stipples, and showcase them from avatar to hero. This look is worth every penny!

Vexy Lines reads a photo as pure light and shade, then redraws every tone as a pattern of strokes, layer by layer, until a raw snapshot becomes clean line art that still looks like the person.

The quiet payoff is the next hire. Save the look once, drop in whoever starts on Monday, and your corporate crypto banknote series stays consistent without a design meeting or a reshoot. The team page, that is.

Read the Vexy Lines case study: Team portrait →

docs.title: Your gradient will not survive the vinyl cutter
docs.text:
Airbrushed lettering dies at the vinyl cutter: no edge to follow, no colour to separate. The Vexy Lines lettering case study rebuilds the glow as flat vector structure — halftone stars sized by tone, masked outlines, hand-tuned Béziers. The result cuts cleanly at four feet, separates to spot colours, and stays editable the whole way.

We turned a soft, low-res airbrush mark into ultrasharp vectors using seven Vexy Lines fills. Best part? Not one of them uses an actual gradient or pixel texture!

A halftone fill scatters stars whose size tracks the tone of the original, so the glow becomes dots you can cut. Hand-drawn shells get their outer edge auto-traced, then tightened by hand with the simple Vexy Lines curve editor. We added a teal core by masking and shrinking the outline, plus a darker halftone fill inside the same mask for texture.

Every soft transition is now a hard-edged path or a field of countable marks. That is the difference between a picture of your wordmark, and a wordmark that the machine can actually reproduce.

Read the Vexy Lines case study: Lettering →

docs.title: Poor print produces pretty posters
docs.text:
In 1977, Albert Kapr squeezed poster style out of cheap GDR paper and a one-colour press. The Vexy Lines retro case study scans his SC Dynamo sheet, rebuilds the halftone photo into a vector signal where stroke thickness answers to luminance, and pours one photograph into three posters: faithful linear, colour-soaked, and full brutalist for the scrolling feed.

Here is what happens when you stop worshipping the museum glass and start reverse-engineering it. We scanned the poster, rebuilt the halftoned photo back into continuous tone, then dropped that grayscale image into Vexy Lines.

Out come retro-authentic vector-perfect ultrasized linear halftones! The reverent direction is black on white, the same line-screen idea Kapr used, now vector artwork that scales past anything a 1977 press could dream of printing.

Take the method, bring it into today: Start with a photo, let the lines carry the tone, then decide whether the gig wants faithful, fluorescent, or feral: and let the engine do the redrawing while you do the deciding!

Read the Vexy Lines case study: Retro poster revival →

docs.title: Make your pixels vexy. Play with lines.
docs.text:
Vexy Playlines turns any photo into vector art in the browser: drop an image, pick one of fourteen algorithmic fills, from classic linear or dotted halftones, to stipple, low-poly, wireframe, ASCII. Drag a slider or two, export SVG! Five fills are free with no sign-up, nothing to install; nine more unlock with a FontLab Pass. Try the quick little cousin of our Mac and Windows Vexy Lines app — built for the ten-minute detour that eats an afternoon.

Here’s a live example of Vexy Playlines running right here on this page: switch the fill, move the before-after splitter, and drag the patterns to change its parameters: left, right, up and down!

Playlines takes the pixels from a photo, reads the tone and the edges, and rebuilds the whole thing in front of you as lines or dots or typed characters while you watch. Nudge a parameter and it redraws instantly, so you’re never guessing, you’re steering. What comes out is a real vector file that scales to a phone or a billboard without going soft. But you don’t have to know any of that to enjoy it. Drag until the picture looks right, download it, then drop it into Photoshop or Affinity or PowerPoint.

Vexy Playlines ships with fourteen ways to see the same face. Stipple scatters thousands of dots like a pointillist who never needs a break; Low-Poly shatters the portrait into coloured triangles; Wireframe turns a person into a blueprint. Five of these fills are free for everyone, with SVG export and no sign-up.

The other nine fills unlock with a FontLab Pass. Each download costs a single Vexy Coin, no subscription. One photo, fourteen completely different looks. You’ll end up trying every single one!

Go do it with your own photo: you’ll have real vector art in less time than it took to read this post!
